## Overview

Diabetes and high blood pressure often go together. Here the outcome is a **number**, systolic blood pressure (SBP), so we use **linear regression**: how much higher, on average, is SBP for each year of age, each BMI unit, and in people with type 2 diabetes, holding the others constant?

### Why this class matters

Linear regression is the foundation of most statistical models, including the gene-by-gene models in 4.5 and 4.6. This class also shows that a model can explain little of the variation (a **low R²**) and still estimate a real difference well, and how to **check** a model with its residuals.

### By the end you'll be able to

1. Explain a **coefficient**: the average change in the outcome per unit of a predictor
2. Fit and read models with `lm()`, `tidy()`, and `glance()`
3. Compare models with **R²**, **adjusted R²**, and **AIC**
4. Check a model's **residuals**

### Analysis at a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| ❓ **Question** | Is type 2 diabetes linked to higher SBP, after accounting for age, sex, BMI, and LDL? |
| 🧪 **The analysis** | **Linear regression**, built up step by step, on the same people |
| 🎯 **Why** | SBP is a number; adjusting separates diabetes from age and weight |
| ✅ **What we conclude** | The adjusted difference in SBP (mm Hg), and how much each model explains |
| ⚠️ **What it can't tell us** | Cause, or **untreated** blood pressure: many people take medicine for it |
| 🔗 **Connections** | The logistic version is **3.2**; the same kind of model is used per gene in **4.5** |

## Key concepts

$$\text{SBP} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{BMI} + \dots + \text{error}$$

- Each **coefficient** is the average change in SBP (mm Hg) per unit of that predictor, holding the others constant. For type 2 diabetes (yes/no), it's the average **difference** between the groups.
- **R²**: the share of variation explained (0 to 1). **AIC**: fit vs complexity, lower is better, only on the same data.
- Blood pressure varies a lot from reading to reading, so R² is **low** here. That doesn't make the coefficients wrong.

## Code walk-through

```r
model_data <- fa %>% drop_na(SBP, age10, sex_at_birth, BMI5, LDL10, t2d)   # <1>

m1 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth,                      data = model_data)
m2 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + LDL10,       data = model_data)
m3 <- lm(SBP ~ age10 + sex_at_birth + BMI5 + LDL10 + t2d, data = model_data)   # <2>

bind_rows("1. Age + sex" = glance(m1), "2. + BMI, LDL" = glance(m2),
          "3. + type 2 diabetes" = glance(m3), .id = "model")               # <3>
tidy(m3, conf.int = TRUE)                                                   # <4>
```
1. Every model on the **same people**, as in 3.2.
2. `lm()` fits a linear regression. Model 3 adds type 2 diabetes last, so its coefficient is **adjusted** for everything before it.
3. `glance()` gives one row of fit statistics per model (R², AIC); `bind_rows(.id = "model")` labels them.
4. `tidy()` gives each coefficient with its 95% confidence interval.

## What we found

Results from our test run in October 2026 (CDR v9), 6,397 people.

| Model 3 coefficient | mm Hg (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Age, per 10 years | +2.0 (1.7 to 2.3) |
| Male (vs female) | +2.4 (1.4 to 3.3) |
| BMI, per 5 units | +1.6 (1.3 to 1.9) |
| LDL, per 10 mg/dL | +0.4 (0.2 to 0.5) |
| **Type 2 diabetes** | **+2.8** (1.8 to 3.7) |

| Model | R² | AIC |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Age + sex | 0.026 | 55,334 |
| 2. + BMI, LDL | 0.051 | 55,170 |
| 3. + type 2 diabetes | 0.056 | 55,142 |

- Type 2 diabetes goes with **2.8 mm Hg** higher SBP, after adjustment: real, but modest.
- Even the best model explains only about **6%** of the variation. Blood pressure depends on much more than these variables (and on the moment it was measured).
- The residual plot was centred on zero with an even spread: the model's assumptions look reasonable.

**💬 Discuss:** many people with diabetes take blood pressure medicines. How does that affect the diabetes coefficient? (It makes it **smaller** than the untreated difference: treatment hides part of the link.)

## Instructor notes

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Instructor tip

- The scatter and residual plots show **one dot per person**: keep them in the notebook, not on slides.
- Students often think a low R² means a useless model. Ask: "Is the 2.8 mm Hg wrong because R² is 0.06?" (No: R² measures prediction of individuals, not the accuracy of an average difference.)
:::

## Key takeaways

- Linear regression is for **numeric** outcomes; coefficients are average changes per unit
- A low **R²** doesn't make a coefficient wrong
- Compare models with AIC, on the **same people**
- **Check the residuals**
- **Treatment** can hide a link in observational data
